newsitem.title: JORDAN: Palestinian refugee agency seeks Gulf Arab support.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian refugee agency seeks Gulf Arab support.

text.p: The U.N. agency helping millions of Palestinian refugees said on Thursday it would appeal to wealthy Gulf Arab oil states to help ease an expected $50 million budget deficit next year.
Peter Hansen, Commissioner-General of the U.N. Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA), said donations from the oil producing states accounted for just one percent of UNRWA's revenue. "We
think the rich countries of this region could pull more weight in the donor community," Hansen told a news conference.

He said he would tour in February the six Gulf Arab states, riding a wave of rising oil prices this year, to seek greater commitment, armed with an Arab League recommendation that Gulf states offer the agency greater support.
Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, currently contributes around $1.2 million a year to UNRWA. Norway gives $30 million and Japan over $25 million, Hansen said.

He said if the richer Arab states, together with the flourishing economies of south-east Asia chipped in "we could make a better life for the Palestinians instead of sitting here talking about cuts in our services."

UNRWA, which warned donors in September it was heading for bankruptcy, won pledges at a recent meeting in New York of around $130 million towards the health care, primary education and social welfare it offers to 3.3 million Palestinian refugees from two major Middle East wars.
But it puts total needs for the 1997 budget, including payments in cash and in kind, at $352 million.
Hansen said if donations remained constant next year the agency faced a $50 million to $60 million deficit, and warned that some projects might have to be shelved.

"Donors have reacted positively, but that does not mean that the future is secure," he said. "We have gone far enough with cutting a little here, cutting a little there... We will have to face what sort of amputations must be done of some programmes."
UNRWA says the cost of helping the refugees spirals every year because of their annual population growth of 3.8 percent.
Hansen appealed to Damascus to clarify a decision on the exchange rate governing UNRWA assistance to Palestinian refugees in Syria, which he said could cost the agency over $6 million a year.
He said a Syrian official had announced that UNRWA would no longer be granted the same exchange rate on Syrian currency that embassies and UN organisations are given.

"If we are being put back to the exchange rate of early this year, and requested back payment on top of that, that would cost us $6 million and for next year... we would be set back another $7 million," Hansen said.

"I simply cannot believe that a host country with obligations towards a humanitarian organisation, that is doing its best to provide services to a refugee population in that country, could do such a thing."
